method: In a constant-voltage system every amplifier of a given line voltage produces the same maximum RMS voltage, 70.7 V being the common US standard, 100 V the common European one and 25 V used for short runs, and each loudspeaker transformer carries a primary tap marked in watts at that voltage. Because the taps share the same reference voltage their wattages add, so the total load is the sum of tap watts times the number of loudspeakers on that tap. The amplifier sees that load as an impedance Z = V squared / P and supplies a line current I = P / V, which is why a 70.7 V line works out to about 5,000 / P ohms and why the same tap is a much heavier load on a 25 V line. Each doubling of tap power adds 10 log10(2) = 3.01 dB, so every tap is also shown against a 1 W tap as 10 log10 of its wattage. The headroom allowance becomes a budget of rated power x (1 - headroom / 100), and the smallest amplifier that keeps the allowance is P / (1 - headroom / 100); the 20 percent default is a planning habit covering tap tolerance, transformer insertion loss, cable loss and program peaks, not a requirement of the standard. This is a budget rather than a measurement: cable resistance, transformer saturation, loudspeaker impedance minima with frequency and loudspeaker sensitivity are not modelled, and the figures apply only to constant-voltage outputs, never to 4, 8 or 16 ohm low-impedance loads. Counts are whole numbers from 0 to 999 per tap, amplifier power 1 to 10000 watts, headroom 0 to 50 percent, and a line with no speakers is refused. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
